Tutorial

Source: tutorial.md

Follow the RBBayes practicals for Bradley–Terry comparisons, shared-strength BT–SBM models and Plackett–Luce rankings. Start with the setup below, then run the examples in order alongside the presentation.

Download course files Read the worked tutorial

The ZIP contains an RStudio Project, the editable tutorial, a plain R script and a setup script. No real data need downloading: the package supplies the datasets used in the practicals.

File Use it for
R Markdown tutorial Read explanations and run the labelled chunks in RStudio.
Plain R script Run the same analysis without R Markdown.
Worked HTML Read all the code, figures and output in a browser.
Setup script Install the packages before class.

1. Install R and RStudio

Install R from CRAN first; RBBayes requires R 4.3 or later. Then install RStudio Desktop. R runs the analysis; RStudio provides the editor, Console, plots and project tools.

If both are already installed, open RStudio and check the R version in its Console:

R.version.string

2. Install the build tools

The GitHub installation below builds RBBayes from source, including its C++ code. Install the tools for your operating system before running it.

Windows

Download Rtools from CRAN, choosing the version listed for your R version. Use the installer’s default options, then restart RStudio. Rtools is a separate installer, not an R package: do not use install.packages("Rtools").

macOS

Open the macOS Terminal application and run:

xcode-select --install

Complete the installation dialogue. The Xcode Command Line Tools are sufficient; the full Xcode application is not required. If the tools are already installed, continue to the next step. This command belongs in Terminal, not in the R Console.

Linux

Install the C/C++ build tools and R development headers for your distribution. For Ubuntu or Debian, a system administrator can install build-essential and r-base-dev. Rtools and Xcode are for Windows and macOS respectively.

3. Open a project and check the working directory

  1. Download the course files ZIP above and extract it. Move the extracted RBBayes-tutorial folder somewhere convenient, such as Documents.
  2. Open RBBayes-tutorial.Rproj from that folder in RStudio.
  3. In the RStudio Console, run:
getwd()
list.files()

getwd() should end in RBBayes-tutorial. The file list should include RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd, RBBayes-tutorial.R and install-packages.R. An RStudio Project sets the working directory to its own folder, so paths in the examples refer to this project rather than the Downloads folder.

If you downloaded individual files

Put them together in one folder. In RStudio select File → New Project → Existing Directory, browse to that folder and choose Create Project. Open the resulting .Rproj file when you return to the practicals.

If you are working without an RStudio Project

Set the working directory explicitly to the folder containing your downloaded files. For example, this creates a tutorial folder under your home directory:

tutorial_dir <- file.path(path.expand("~"), "RBBayes-tutorial")
dir.create(tutorial_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
setwd(tutorial_dir)
getwd()

Move the downloaded .Rmd and .R files into the folder printed by getwd(). Alternatively, use setwd("/the/actual/path/to/your/tutorial-folder"), replacing the example path with your own. On Windows, forward slashes work in R paths, for example "C:/Users/your-name/Documents/RBBayes-tutorial".

4. Install the R packages

Run the following in the RStudio Console, once. An internet connection is needed for installation. The same commands are in install-packages.R.

# Run once in RStudio's R Console after installing the system build tools.
install.packages(c("remotes", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
remotes::install_github("lapo-santi/RBBayes", upgrade = "never")

remotes installs the GitHub version of RBBayes and its required dependencies, including dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2. knitr and rmarkdown let you knit the editable tutorial. Accept a personal R library if R asks to create one. Restart the R session after updating an already-loaded RBBayes installation.

For the diagnostic and partition-search sections used in class, also run:

install.packages(c("coda", "bayesplot", "salso"))

coda provides MCMC diagnostics, bayesplot provides posterior plots, and salso supplies the partition search. They are optional: the tutorial skips unavailable diagnostic sections and uses a built-in partition search when salso is absent. Match the packages used in class for matching results.

Check that the installed package has the teaching interface:

library(RBBayes)
packageVersion("RBBayes")
stopifnot("simulate_data" %in% getNamespaceExports("RBBayes"))

5. Open the tutorial and run the code

In RStudio, choose File → Open File and select RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd inside your project. It opens in the Source pane. Run the packages chunk first, then continue through the labelled chunks from top to bottom.

Use the green Run button beside a chunk. To run selected lines, use Run or Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on macOS). The Console shows text output; figures appear inline or in the Plots pane, depending on your RStudio settings. See RStudio’s code-execution guide.

The sequence matches the practical sessions:

  1. BT: simulate individual strengths, prepare comparisons, fit and inspect normalised posterior strengths.
  2. BT–SBM: after the block-model theory session, simulate shared block strengths and study the partition and its uncertainty; then analyse ATP data.
  3. PL: prepare rankings and fit a Plackett–Luce model.

The complete tutorial includes the diagnostics and appendix. The short code examples further down this page use the same chunks.

If you prefer a plain R script

Open RBBayes-tutorial.R and run its named sections in order. It contains the analysis code, with optional diagnostics guarded by package-availability checks. To run the whole file and display its output from the Console:

source("RBBayes-tutorial.R", echo = TRUE)

Produce your own HTML output

With the .Rmd open, click Knit. Or run:

rmarkdown::render("RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd")

The result, RBBayes-tutorial.html, is created beside your source file and opens in a browser or viewer. Rendering runs the model fits again and can take a few minutes. Results can vary with R/package versions and optional packages; sessionInfo() at the end records your environment.

BT: individual player strengths

Begin with one generating strength per player. No block model is needed here.

lambda <- exp(seq(log(12), 0, length.out = 20)) # One strength per player.
edges <- simulate_data(
  model = "bt", latent_strength = lambda,
  item_labels = paste("Player", seq_along(lambda)),
  matches_per_pair = 20, seed = 101, format = "edgelist"
)
edges |> slice_head(n = 6) |> knitr::kable()

tennis <- as_bt_data(edges, format = "edgelist")
tennis

bt_fit <- fit_model(
  tennis,
  bt_model(shape_lambda = 2),
  mcmc_control(iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 12)
)
bt_fit
summary(bt_fit)

bt_strength <- strength_summary(bt_fit)
plot_strength_summary(bt_fit)

BT–SBM: shared block strengths

Introduce generating blocks after the BT–SBM theory session. Block sizes may be equal or different; the comments show both forms.

edges_sbm <- simulate_data(
  model = "bt-sbm",
  n_blocks = 4, latent_strength = c(12, 6, 2, 1), # One strength per block.
  players_per_block = 5, # Unequal sizes are also allowed: c(3, 4, 5, 8).
  matches_per_pair = 20, seed = 101, format = "edgelist"
)
tennis_sbm <- as_bt_data(edges_sbm, format = "edgelist")
truth <- attr(edges_sbm, "truth")
edges_sbm |> slice_head(n = 6) |> knitr::kable()

sbm_model <- bt_sbm_model(
  shape_lambda = 2,
  item_clustering = gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.5)
)
sbm_model
sbm_fit <- fit_model(tennis_sbm, sbm_model,
                     mcmc_control(iter = 10000, warmup = 5000, seed = 2))
summary(sbm_fit)

posterior_K_table(sbm_fit)

PL: ranked observations

The same fitting interface also handles rankings.

sushi <- sushi_toy(n_rankings = 40, rank_length = 5, seed = 3)
sushi
head(sushi$rankings, 3)
plot_ranking_positions(sushi)

pl_fit <- fit_model(sushi, pl_model(shape_lambda = 1),
                    mcmc_control(iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, seed = 4))
summary(pl_fit)

plot_strength_summary(pl_fit)

Read the complete worked tutorial for posterior uncertainty, MCMC diagnostics, the ATP example and exercises.

If something does not work

What you see What to check
could not find function "simulate_data" Restart R, reinstall RBBayes from GitHub, then run library(RBBayes).
A compiler error mentioning g++, make or clang++ Complete the build-tools step for your operating system.
there is no package called ... Install that package in the R Console, then rerun the packages chunk.
cannot open file or file not found Check getwd() and list.files(); open the tutorial’s .Rproj or choose the correct folder.
An object such as tennis or bt_fit is missing Run the preceding tutorial chunks first.
file.copy() returns FALSE The destination may already exist or be unwritable. Use the direct downloads above or a fresh project folder; preserve your edited copy.

Find the copy bundled with the package

The website downloads do not require searching your R library. If you already installed RBBayes, the package also contains the tutorial. Installation stores it inside the package; it does not create a Desktop file or open a Source tab.

Read that installed HTML with:

browseURL(system.file("tutorial", "RBBayes-tutorial.html",
                      package = "RBBayes", mustWork = TRUE))

Copy its editable source into your current working directory and open it:

source_file <- system.file("tutorial", "RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd",
                           package = "RBBayes", mustWork = TRUE)
if (!file.exists("RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd")) {
  stopifnot(file.copy(source_file, "RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd"))
}
file.edit("RBBayes-tutorial.Rmd")

An existing file is kept. Use a fresh folder if you need a new copy without replacing your work. This bundled file is separate from the package’s registered vignettes, so it does not appear in vignette() listings.
